## Vulnerability Details

1. In the call to `[openCdp()]` external function of the <EbtcLeverageZapRouter> contract, there's a collateral value based on the margin Amount that is transferred to the ZapRouterBase contract from the user. This represents the user's collateral put up to open the cdp... See #L181 of `EbtcLeverageZapRouter::openCdp` function. 
 + The contract then calls the internal [_openCdp] function, with the fifth param as this margin collateral value put up
2. In the internal [_openCdp()] , the function does not do anything with the user's put up collateral.. 
 + In fact, the put-up collateral isnot used anywhere within this function.. it's absolutely neglected..
 + `# instead of setting the openCdpForOperation.stEthToDeposit = collateralValue , it mistakenly sets it to stEthDepositAmount.` Now this is a user input parameter that can be set to any arbitrary value.
 + The only check associated with this stEthDepositAmount parameter is that it's supposed to be greater than 2.2e18, which means a user can set that input to a really high value, like type(uint256).max.

3. The contract then calls the internal [LeverageZapRouterBase::_openCdpForOperation] function with params of the newly set values for the openCdpForOperation struct.
 + This in turn calls the internal [LeverageMacroBase::_doOperation].
 + There is a return array that's passed into the [_doOperation] function as a parameter. This return array is obtained via the call to [_getPostCheckParams] with an interesting parameter here:

 `<stETH.getSharesByPooledEth(openCdpForOperation.stEthToDeposit)>   =====>>>>>> because of the inflated value set to this, the return shares will be extremely high...... Now, this function calculates the collateral shares using (this extremely high value * tradeData.collValidationBufferBPS)/ 10000, and the resultant gets assigned to PostCheckParams.expectedCollateral value`.....

4. Now, because we are opening a cdp position, the flashloan type to execute inside the `[_doOperation]` function will be stEth. This will call the flashloan function on the ActivePool contract. 
 + In the flashloan return callback from the ActivePool Contract to the leverageMacroBase contract, there's a call to `_handleOperation` which in turn calls `_openCdpForCallback(encoded_Data)`. The encoded_Data includes the eBTC token to mint as debt, and the put up inflated collateral <stETHToDeposit>.
+ Now inside the `[_openCdpForCallback]`, there's a call to the `borrowerOperations::openCdpFor --> _openCdp` function with params of the encoded_Data including the: `<stETHToDeposit>` inflated arbitrary value that was set from the beginning in the `EbtcLeverageZapRouter::openCdpFor` function .

5. Now this `borrowerOperations::_openCdp` uses the inflated collateral shares of the user as the user's put up collateral margin, which in truth, isn't. Look at some instances it utilizes this artificially inflated value
+ OpenCdpLocals memory vars;
  `vars.netStEthBalance = _calcNetStEthBalance(stETHToDeposit)`;

+ It even calculates a user's collateral shares based on this inflated value:
 uint256 _netCollAsShares = collateral.getSharesByPooledEth(`vars.netStEthBalance`)

+ It even calculates a user's ICR based on this artificially inflated value:
  vars.ICR = EbtcMath._compute(`vars.netStETHBalance`, vars.debt, vars.price)


6. Now after all checks, it finally initializes the cdp for the user within the borrowerOperations contract by calling `cdpManager::initializeCdp` function,and sets the user's collateral shares to this inflated arbitrary value
```
        cdpManager.initializeCdp(
            _cdpId,
            vars.debt,
            _netCollAsShares,
            _liquidatorRewardShares,
            _borrower
        );
```

7. Now, the malicious user armed with an infinite number of collateral shares, can close his position to receive this number of shares although he really didnot put up that much collateral, effectively stealing from the protocol including the shares of other users.

8. Malicious user puts up a 100 wei of stEth as the collateral stEth margin amount. However, he sets the `stEthDepositAmount` parameter to an extremely high value, say 1_000_000 e18. To write this value as his collateral shares in the cdp he is about to open, he sets the total expected debt parameter to be 1000 wei (This is because there is a require check that the expected debt should be 0 or greater than 1000). He also sets the stEthLoanAmount, ie, the flashloan amount to any value > 0, say 50 wei too. Now, this leveraged cpd position will be opened with user's collateral as 1_000_000e18. The malicious user can then later close his cdp position to take away his associated collateral, in this case, his 1_000_000e18 even though he didnot put up this amount of collateral in the first place.  


## Impact
1. Now, armed with this high collateral shares, comes with very high collateralization Ratio. Now with this extremely high ICR associated with the malicious user's cdp, he can borrow an extremely high amount of eBTC tokens from the protocol (even when he sets the flash loan amount to a very low value), and yet still his ICR will be above the minimum, effectively stealing the eBTC tokens from the protocol. 

2. When malicious user calls `EbtcLeverageZapRouter::closeCdp()`, his put up collateral is sent back to him, and his position is closed. However, the collateral shares that will be sent to the malicious user is the inflated collateral he had set when opening the leveraged position. The withdrawal will pass as he won't have any bad debt in the protocol. This will effectively have led to the stolen of either protocol shares or shares of other users or both. 


3. Malicious user can even DoS the protocol, by preventing other legitimate users from opening a position. 
 + When a user opens a leveraged position, and `cdpManager::initiliazeCdp` is called, `totalStaked` state variable of the `CdpManagerStorage.sol` contract is updated by being incremented by the user's cdp.stake value. See below#

`https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-protocol/packages/contracts/contracts/CdpManager.sol#L947`

`https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-protocol/packages/contracts/contracts/CdpManagerStorage.sol#L426-L430`

+ Malicious user can attempt to push the `uint256 totalStaked` state variable to an extremely high value that is almost equal to type(uint256).max by opening 2 or more seperate leveraged positions.

+ Now, when legitimate users attempts to open a leveraged position, with their put up collateral margin, the `totalStaked` state variable will overflow, and the transaction to open a position will revert, effectively DoSing the protocol permanently.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-zap-router/src/EbtcLeverageZapRouter.sol#L321-L329

# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Summary

There is a wrong validation in the `requireSingularMarginChange` function in the EbtcLeverageZapRouter contract. It only checks that either of the 2 parameters should be 0. However, it fails to check also that both of the 2 parameters cannot be 0, that is, one of the parameters must be 0, while the other is a non-zero.

And due to its usage in `EbtcLeverageZapRouter::_adjustCdp` with respect to <marginIncrease> and <marginDecrease> calculation, Attacker can weaponize this vulnerability to clear his debt to the minimum debt (1000) without any repayment, and hence increase his position's ICR as a result. 

## Vulnerability Details

1. In the external `[adjustCdp]` function, if AdjustCdpParams.stEthMarginBalance is set to 0, there won't be any transfer of stEth from the caller, as the condition 
won't be true. The external then calls the internal `_adjustCdp` function.

Assuming the following values for the parameters below...

AdjustCdpParams.stEthBalanceChange = 0;

AdjustCdpParams.stEthMarginBalance = 0;

AdjustCdpParams.debtChange = value greater than 1000, but 1000 less than my original debt.Say, if original debt is 15_000, AdjustCdpParams.debtChange <= 14000;

AdjustCdpParams.isStEthBalanceIncrease = false;

AdjustCdpParams.isDebtIncrease = false;


2. Inside the internal `[_adjustCdp]` function, all the `requireZeroOrMinAdjustment()` checks will pass. The code then pulls the original debt and original collateral shares associated with the caller's cdpId from the cdpManager contract.

3. With the values assumed above for the AdjustCdpParams, both `uint256 marginDecrease` and `uint256 marginIncrease` will be equal to 0. Now, the check `requireNonZeroAdjustment()` will pass because AdjustCdpParams.debtChange is non-zero. Also, the check `requireSingularMarginChange` will also pass because both `uint256 marginIncrease` and `uint256 marginDecrease` are 0. 

`However, the vulnerability lies in the fact that the <requireSingularMarginChange> only checks that one of the parameters should be 0. So, both parameters can be 0, and because of the logical OR operator, the check will pass. The code fails to check that both cannot be 0 too. In fact, it's clear that, the intended functionality is to ensure that only one of <marginIncrease> or <marginDecrease> is 0, and the other is a non-zero. But this check is inefficient`


3. The code then calls the internal `[_adjustCdpOperation]` function with cdp parameters set as below:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-zap-router/src/EbtcLeverageZapRouter.sol#L440-L447

Now inside the [_adjustCdpOperation] function, there is a calculation of "newDebt" and "newCollateral". 

 + Because AdjustCdpParams.isDebtIncrease = cdp.isDebtIncrease = false, the else part of the "newDebt" calculation will execute:
      newDebt = debt - cdp.EBTCChange(AdjustCdpParams.debtChange);

   Now, because Attacker carefully chose the debtChange value, the result of the newDebt calculation will almost be equal to 1000 or near 1000, thereby overwritting attacker's original debt to a very low value than before...

 + The new collateral calculation is dependent on the value of `stEthBalanceIncrease` (marginIncrease). Note also that, `stEthBalanceDecrease` = marginDecrease = 0. 
 Now, because this "stEthBalanceIncrease" is 0, the else part of the `new coll` will execute:
    newColl = coll - stEth.getSharesByPooledEth(cdp.stEthBalanceDecrease);
=>> newColl = coll - 0 = coll

Now, the new collateral remains the same as with the original collateral, whilst the new Debt has decreased significantly.


4. Before calling the [_doOperation] internal function, it calls the `_getPostCheckParams` function with the newDebt and newColl variables as parameters. This function sets the expectedDebt and expectedColl values to the values of newDebt and newColl respectively. 


5. The code then further calls the internal `_doOperation` function on the LeverageMacroBase contract. Now, because cdp.isDebtIncrease is set to false, the flashloan type to execute will be the eBTC token flashloan.. The flashloan amount is insignificant to this attack, as any amount can be used to launch the attack, even 1 wei.
  + Now this calls the flashloan function on the BorrowerOperations contract, which further returns the onFlashloan callback to this leverageMacroBase contract. Now inside this onFlashloan callback is a call to `handleOperation()`, which in turns calls the `_adjustCdpCallback` function. 

         `_handleOperation(operation);`

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-protocol/packages/contracts/contracts/LeverageMacroBase.sol#L426

      `} else if (operation.operationType == OperationType.AdjustCdpOperation) {
                     _adjustCdpCallback(operation.OperationData);`



https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-protocol/packages/contracts/contracts/LeverageMacroBase.sol#L340-L341


 +    + Now, this `_adjustCdpCallback` calls the `_adjustCdpWithColl` function on the BorrowerOperations contract. This in turn calls the `_adjustCdpInternal` function too.

+ Now, this will pass the checks inside this function too:
  1. requireZeroOrMinAdjustment();

  2. requireZeroCollChange();

  3. requireNonZeroAdjustment();

  + Now, a new ICR is set for the cdpId using this reduced debt and original collateral. Because, the debt was reduced significantly, but the original collateral shares stayed the same, the new ICR will increase significantly. 

 + Also, this function calls the `cdpManager.update()`. This `cdpManager.update()` function overwrites the original debt, and original collateral shares associated with the attacker's cdpId with this new value of debt. 


6. The postChecks inside the `_doOperation` function will pass too.

  https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-protocol/packages/contracts/contracts/LeverageMacroBase.sol#L219-L228


  + It checks the expectedDebt against the now original debt from the cdpManager contract, and this will pass, because expectedDebt = ICdpManagerData.Cdp.debt

  + It also checks the new collateral against the now recorded collateral from the CdpManager contract, and that will pass too, because expectedColl >= ICdpManagerData.Cdp.coll (expectedColl and ICdpManagerData.Cdp.coll are equal).


7. With a new increased ICR, attacker will be allowed to borrow more even though he didnot increase his collateral shares, neither did he repay his debt.


## Impact
1. Attacker has been able to clear his debt to the minimum debt with 0 repayment.

2. With a new increased ICR, attacker can borrow more from the protocol.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Effective recommended mitigation will be to also check that both marginIncrease and marginDecrease cannot be 0.  You can refine the _requireSingularMarginChange() function to match the one below:

```

function _requireSingularMarginChange(
        uint256 _stEthMarginIncrease,
        uint256 _stEthMarginDecrease
    ) internal pure {
        require(
            (_stEthMarginIncrease == 0 && _stEthMarginDecrease > 0) || (stEthMarginIncrease > 0 && _stEthMarginDecrease == 0),
            "EbtcLeverageZapRouter: Cannot add and withdraw margin in same operation"
        );
    }

```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-zap-router/src/EbtcLeverageZapRouter.sol#L390-L401


# Vulnerability details


## Proof of Concept
When a CDP is opened, the contract checks that the initial collateral deposited meets the minimum requirement of 2 stETH. This is done through the [_requireAtLeastMinNetStEthBalance](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-zap-router/src/EbtcLeverageZapRouter.sol#L217) function, which compares the total `stETH` deposit amount minus a predefined reward (`LIQUIDATOR_REWARD`) against a minimum threshold. However, when adjusting a CDP, the contract does not perform a similar check to ensure that the remaining collateral after the adjustment still meets this minimum requirement.

The [adjustCdp](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-zap-router/src/EbtcLeverageZapRouter.sol#L390) functions allow for various operations that might change both the collateral and debt of a CDP. These operations include increasing or decreasing the collateral, changing the debt, and possibly withdrawing some of the collateral as margin. Since there is no check to ensure that the remaining collateral after such adjustments is at least 2 stETH, a user could theoretically reduce their collateral below this threshold through these adjustments. This vulnerability could lead to scenarios where the collateral is insufficient to cover the debt, potentially leading to liquidation events.
### Example Scenario
Consider a scenario where a user opens a CDP with $`4 stETH`$ as collateral, meeting the minimum requirement. Later, the user decides to adjust their CDP by reducing their collateral to $`1.5 stETH`$. Without the enforcement of the minimum collateral requirement during adjustments, the contract would not prevent this action, even though it results in a violation of the minimum collateral rule.
## Impact
Users can reduce their collateral below the required threshold. This could lead to a situation where the collateral is insufficient to cover the debt, posing a significant risk to the stability and security of the CDP mechanism.
## Tools Used
Manual
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The contract should implement checks in the `adjustCdp` functions to ensure that the remaining collateral after an adjustment is at least equal to the minimum required collateral. This can be achieved by recalculating the total collateral after the adjustment and comparing it against the minimum requirement. If the new total is below the threshold, the transaction should revert with an appropriate error message.

# Lines of code

# Vulnerability details

## Proof of Concept
The core of the issue lies in the calculation performed within the [_requireAtLeastMinNetStEthBalance](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-zap-router/src/EbtcLeverageZapRouter.sol#L217) function. The function aims to ensure that the net `stETH` balance of a CDP, calculated as `_stEthDepositAmount - LIQUIDATOR_REWARD`, does not fall below a predefined minimum threshold [(MIN_NET_STETH_BALANCE)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-zap-router/src/ZapRouterBase.sol#L144C30-L144C52). This calculation is intended to account for the liquidator reward, which is a mechanism to incentivize liquidators to act when a CDP falls below a certain health factor.

However, the subtraction of `LIQUIDATOR_REWARD` from `_stEthDepositAmount` assumes that the liquidator reward is not already included in `_stEthDepositAmount`. This assumption may not always hold true, especially in scenarios where the `_stEthDepositAmount` encompasses the liquidator reward as part of the total `stETH` collateral amount. In such cases, subtracting the liquidator reward again would result in a negative net `stETH` balance, which contradicts the function's purpose and could lead to erroneous rejections of valid transactions.
Let's explore two hypothetical scenarios that illustrate the potential vulnerability in the `_requireAtLeastMinNetStEthBalance` function.
### Scenario 1: Incorrect Liquidator Reward Deduction
Background: Alice wants to open a CDP (Collateralized Debt Position) using the `openCdp` function. She deposits 5 stETH as collateral and intends to borrow 2 ETH through a flash loan. The liquidator reward is set to 0.2 stETH.

Current Implementation:

- Alice's `_stEthDepositAmount` is 5 stETH.
- The liquidator reward is 0.2 stETH.
- The function calculates the net stETH balance as $5 stETH - 0.2 stETH = 4.8 stETH$.
Issue: The function checks if the net `stETH` balance is greater than or equal to `MIN_NET_STETH_BALANCE` (which is 2 stETH). Since 4.8 stETH is greater than 2 stETH, the transaction proceeds. However, because the liquidator reward is not accounted for in the calculation, Alice could potentially benefit from a liquidation event without having the required minimum net stETH balance.

### Scenario 2: Double Deduction of Liquidator Reward
Background: Bob decides to adjust his CDP using the `adjustCdp` function. He increases his collateral by 1 stETH, bringing his total to 6 stETH. The liquidator reward remains at 0.2 stETH.

Current Implementation:

- Bob's `_stEthDepositAmount` is increased to 6 stETH.
- The function calculates the net stETH balance as $6 stETH - 0.2 stETH = 5.8 stETH$.
Issue: Similar to the first scenario, the function checks if the net stETH balance is greater than or equal to `MIN_NET_STETH_BALANCE`. Since 5.8 stETH is greater than 2 stETH, the transaction proceeds. However, if the liquidator reward were somehow deducted twice (either due to a mistake in the code or misunderstanding of the logic), the net stETH balance could incorrectly appear to meet the minimum requirement.
## Impact
Alice could potentially benefit from a liquidation event without having the required minimum net stETH balance.

## Tools Used
Manual
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Instead of subtracting the liquidator reward from the `_stEthDepositAmount`, the function should verify that the `_stEthDepositAmount` plus the liquidator reward meets or exceeds the `MIN_NET_STETH_BALANCE`.

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-zap-router/src/EbtcLeverageZapRouter.sol#L214

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In the `EbtcLeverageZapRouter` contract, from the functions of `_openCdp()`, `_closeCdp()` and `_adjustCdp()` we can see they are using `nonReentrant`, this means the protocol is designed as not allowing reentrance into the methods above.

However, this `nonReentrant` only works for its residing contract. Since this protocol has two separate user touchpoint router contracts (`EbtcLeverageZapRouter` and `EbtcZapRouter`), hence, a malicious user can still perform a reentrancy-ish operation which is supposed to be forbidden by the protocol. I'll demonstrate how it is done in the POC section below. This issue can let the user get around the protocol's designed non-reentrancy, and mess up operations with CDP which were supposed to be disallowed actions.

## Proof of Concept
1. The user can start with the adjust/close/open CDP related function in the contract `EbtcLeverageZapRouter`. Such functions accept arbitrary data `_tradeData`, this is what the malicious user can utilize;
2. These functions will make a series of call stack, they will go to the `LeverageMacroBase` contract, thru `_doOperation`=>`_handleOperation`=>`_doSwaps`=>`_doSwap`
3. Here in `_doSwap` the call to an arbitrary external contract is happening. The user can prepare a malicious external contract as the `swapData.addressForSwap`, when being called, the malicious contract will call the other router contract `EbtcZapRouter` and it can totally get into the adjust/close/open CDP related function again because there is no reentrancy guard in that contract.
4. This kind of reentrancy attack cannot have more than 1 extra round because it does not get the reentrancy point again for a 2nd round. However, it can enter for 1 extra round so it already breaks the protocol's design.


## Tools Used
Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Deploy a separate contract functioning as the Global Reentrancy Guard, this contract holds a state variable as the lock status. All necessary functions in the multiple user touchpoint contracts come here to toggle the lock and read the universal lock status, so it makes any cross-contract reentrancy impossible.


## Assessed type

Reentrancy

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-protocol/packages/contracts/contracts/LeverageMacroBase.sol#L464-L470


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Users can re-enter Router through DEX to reduce the fee of flash loan from BorrowerOperations.

## Proof of Concept
Under normal business, if the user adjusts the CDP through the Router, [he or she needs to perform flash loan through borrowerOperations/activePool](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-zap-router/src/EbtcLeverageZapRouter.sol#L436-L438). The more CDPs you want to change, the more tokens you need to borrow. [The greater the number of flash loans, the more fees there will be](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-protocol/packages/contracts/contracts/BorrowerOperations.sol#L1128-L1133).
```solidity
        _adjustCdpOperation({
            _cdpId: _cdpId,
            _flType: _params.isDebtIncrease ? FlashLoanType.stETH : FlashLoanType.eBTC,
```

However, users can make the fee smaller by reentry. Users can borrow smaller flash loans and adjust the CDP again through reentry. In this way, you only need one flash loan and can perform multiple operations.

Specifically, the steps are as follows (the following operations are completed in one transaction):
1. The user first performs the normal adjustCdp operation to lend amountX eBTC.
2. When the [_doSwap function is executed, DEX will be called](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-protocol/packages/contracts/contracts/LeverageMacroBase.sol#L464-L470). According to the documentation, this is 0x or 1inch.
3. Taking 1inch as an example, since [calldataForSwap](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-protocol/packages/contracts/contracts/LeverageMacroBase.sol#L469C13-L469C37) is defined by the user, [swap](https://www.codeslaw.app/contracts/ethereum/0x1111111254eeb25477b68fb85ed929f73a960582?file=AggregationRouterV5.sol&start=973) can be called here, and then the user's own contract is called through [the call function in swap](https://www.codeslaw.app/contracts/ethereum/0x1111111254eeb25477b68fb85ed929f73a960582?file=AggregationRouterV5.sol&start=1046).
4. After the user calls any dex in his contract to exchange eBTC for stETH, he can then call the router again to lend out amountX of eBTC.
5. In this way, users can perform multiple operations with one flash loan, saving the fees of flash loans.
```solidity
    function _doSwap(SwapOperation memory swapData) internal {

        _ensureNotSystem(swapData.addressForSwap);

        IERC20(swapData.tokenForSwap).safeApprove(
            swapData.addressForApprove,
            swapData.exactApproveAmount
        );

        (bool success, ) = excessivelySafeCall(
            swapData.addressForSwap,
            gasleft(),
            0,
            0,
            swapData.calldataForSwap
        );
        require(success, "Call has failed");
```

Users can also use Uni's flash loan function to re-enter when calling a pool such as Uni. The fee is only the swap fee and there is no flash loan fee.

Manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add a re-enter lock to the router.

## Impact

The contract may behave in an unexpected manner

## Proof of concept

[https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/main/ebtc-zap-router/src/ZapRouterBase.sol#L38](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/main/ebtc-zap-router/src/ZapRouterBase.sol#L38)

When a user tries to open or adjust a CDP using native ETH or WETH, the asset is converted to stETH by being deposited on Lido using the `_depositRawEthIntoLido()` internal function.

Lido has [2 ways](https://etherscan.io/address/0x17144556fd3424edc8fc8a4c940b2d04936d17eb#code) to prevent users from staking their ETH :
1. The contract is paused
2. The stake limit has been reached

If Lido ends up in one of the 2 situations above, all the deposits will essentially revert, whether it is through the use of the `fallback()` function (which eBTC uses) or through the `submit()` function.

In the current implementation, since the low-level call return value is not checked, the contract will revert directly, in an attempt to deposit the assets, which could lead to potential unexpected behaviors in the future.

*in an ideal situation, the transaction will revert later on anyway because the execution flow will try to pull stETH from the router which is not supposed to hold any token*

## Tools used

Manual analysis

## Recommended mitigation steps

There are 2 options :

1. Make sure to check the return value of the deposit to Lido in the `_depositRawEthIntoLido()` internal function

```diff
function _depositRawEthIntoLido(uint256 _initialETH) internal returns (uint256) {
    // check before-after balances for 1-wei corner case
    uint256 _balBefore = stEth.balanceOf(address(this));
    // TODO call submit() with a referral?
-   payable(address(stEth)).call{value: _initialETH}("");
+   (bool success,) = payable(address(stEth)).call{value: _initialETH}("");
+   require(success, "Can't stake on Lido");
    uint256 _deposit = stEth.balanceOf(address(this)) - _balBefore;
    return _deposit;
}
```

2. Call the `submit()` function on the stETH contract instead of using its `fallback()` function which will revert in case the deposit fails.

An invariant is violated in the current implementation. The Position Manager Permit, which grants access to user CDPs, is not revoked after each operation as required.             _positionManagerPermit.v,

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

This could allow users to artificially inflate the amount of stETH or wstETH they receive when closing their CDP. An attacker could exploit this to drain excess collateral from the protocol, leading to losses. This has a direct impact on the protocol's funds and the relative ease of exploitation.

## Proof of Concept

Look at the `_closeCdp` function of the `EbtcLeverageZapRouter` contract: https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-zap-router/src/EbtcLeverageZapRouter.sol#L276-L308

```solidity
function _closeCdp(
    bytes32 _cdpId,
    bytes calldata _positionManagerPermit,
    bool _useWstETH,
    TradeData calldata _tradeData
) internal nonReentrant {
    // ... (omitted code for brevity)

    uint256 _zapStEthBalanceBefore = stEth.balanceOf(address(this));
    _closeCdpOperation({
        _cdpId: _cdpId,
        _debt: debt,
        _tradeData: _tradeData
    });
    uint256 _zapStEthBalanceAfter = stEth.balanceOf(address(this));
    uint256 _stETHDiff = _zapStEthBalanceAfter - _zapStEthBalanceBefore;

    _transferStEthToCaller(_cdpId, EthVariantZapOperationType.CloseCdp, _useWstETH, _stETHDiff);
}
```

As seeen, the function calculates the amount of stETH to return based on the difference in the contract's stETH balance before and after the `_closeCdpOperation`. This approach is vulnerable to manipulation.

Let's consider a scenario:
1. Alice wants to close her CDP, which has 100 stETH as collateral.
2. Just before Alice's transaction is processed, an attacker Bob sends 50 stETH directly to the `EbtcLeverageZapRouter` contract.
3. Alice's `_closeCdp` function executes:
   - `_zapStEthBalanceBefore` is recorded as 50 (the amount Bob sent)
   - The CDP is closed, releasing Alice's 100 stETH
   - `_zapStEthBalanceAfter` is now 150 (Bob's 50 + Alice's 100)
   - `_stETHDiff` is calculated as 150 - 50 = 100
4. The function transfers 100 stETH to Alice (or the equivalent in wstETH if `_useWstETH` is true)
5. Bob withdraws his 50 stETH in a separate transaction

Finally, Alice receives 100 stETH instead of the 50 stETH she should have received (assuming 50% of the collateral was used to repay the debt). The protocol loses 50 stETH.


## Tools Used
Manual code analysis

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

The contract should not rely on balance differences. Instead, it should track the exact amount of collateral released from the CDP during the closure operation.

# Vulnerability details



## Impact

This can result in users paying higher fees than intended and having their CDPs reflect a higher debt than the actual eBTC received. 

## Proof of Concept

The problem is present in both the `_openCdpForCallback` and `_adjustCdpCallback` functions. Lookking at the `_openCdpForCallback` function: https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-zap-router/src/LeverageZapRouterBase.sol#L276-L292

```solidity
function _openCdpForCallback(bytes memory data) internal override {
    if (zapFeeBPS > 0) {
        OpenCdpForOperation memory flData = abi.decode(data, (OpenCdpForOperation));

        bytes32 _cdpId = borrowerOperations.openCdpFor(
            flData.eBTCToMint,
            flData._upperHint,
            flData._lowerHint,
            flData.stETHToDeposit,
            flData.borrower
        );

        IERC20(address(ebtcToken)).safeTransfer(zapFeeReceiver, flData.eBTCToMint * zapFeeBPS / BPS);
    } else {
        super._openCdpForCallback(data);
    }
}
```

CDP is opened for the full `flData.eBTCToMint` amount, but then a fee is deducted from this amount and sent to the `zapFeeReceiver`. This means:

- The user's CDP reflects a debt of `flData.eBTCToMint`.
-  The user actually receives `flData.eBTCToMint - (flData.eBTCToMint * zapFeeBPS / BPS)`.

For exxample, if a user wants to mint 100 eBTC and the `zapFeeBPS` is 50 (0.5%):
1. The CDP is opened with a debt of 100 eBTC.
2. 0.5 eBTC is sent to the `zapFeeReceiver`.
3. The user only receives 99.5 eBTC.

This could be costly in scenarios where the user is close to the liquidation threshold. They might believe they have more buffer than they actually do, potentially leading to unexpected liquidations as the case may be.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Recalculate the eBTC amount to mint or adjust before performing the CDP operation, subtracting the fee amount first. Then, open or adjust the CDP with this reduced amount, ensuring the CDP's debt accurately reflects the eBTC the user receives. Finally, transfer the calculated fee to the `zapFeeReceiver`.


The failure to revoke the position manager permit after each operation leaves users' CDPs vulnerable to unauthorized access. This breaks the main security invariant and could potentially allow the `ZapRouter` contract or malicious actors to manipulate users' positions without their consent in subsequent transactions.

## Proof of Concept
In the ZapRouterBase.sol contract, there's a function to grant the position manager permit: https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-zap-router/src/ZapRouterBase.sol#L115-L133

```solidity
function _permitPositionManagerApproval(
    IBorrowerOperations borrowerOperations,
    PositionManagerPermit memory _positionManagerPermit
) internal {
    try
        borrowerOperations.permitPositionManagerApproval(
            msg.sender,
            address(this),
            IPositionManagers.PositionManagerApproval.OneTime,
            _positionManagerPermit.deadline,
            _positionManagerPermit.v,
            _positionManagerPermit.r,
            _positionManagerPermit.s
        )
    {} catch {

    }
}
```

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-zap-router/src/EbtcLeverageZapRouter.sol#L403-L467


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

`EbtcLeverageZapRouter` is missing the ability to both perform debt decrease and collateral increase, which will prevent users from having granular control over their CDP positions.

## Proof of Concept

Due to the limitation of `EbtcLeverageZapRouter` to perform only `stETH` or `eBTC` flash loans, not both at the same time, users have no native way to both decrease their debt (burn `eBTC`) and increase their collateral (add `stETH`). There can be scenarios when `EbtcZapRouter` is not enough to perform these 2 actions in unison. 

Consider the example of `stETH` price crash and the system has entered recovery mode. Alice has CDP with 1 `eBTC`, 21 `stETH`, and her CR has fallen below 103%. now she has 3 options:

1. `Decrease her debt`
    1. Pros
        1. Improved CR, avoiding liquidation
    2. Cons
        1. Receive collateral tokens at a very low price
2. `Increase her collateral`
    1. Pros
        1. Improved CR, avoiding liquidation
    2. Cons 
        1. Provide all the needed collateral from herself, since no eBTC can be borrowed against it, or simply has to add a lot of `stETH`, to get `eBTC` which will be used to repay the flash loan, but this will make her pay higher rebase fee due to the increased CDP stake.
3. `Decrease her debt + increase her collateral` **atomically with flash loans** through `EbtcLeverageZapRouter`
    1. Pros

# Vulnerability details

The `openCdpWithWstEth` function allows users to specify the `_stEthDepositAmount` independently of the actual collateral converted from `_wstEthMarginBalance`. This can lead to situations where a CDP  is created with insufficient collateral. The  logic does not enforce that the converted margin balance (`_collVal`) matches the specified deposit amount (`_stEthDepositAmount`),resulting in under-collateralized positions.


## Impact
This will lead to the creation of CDPs that do not have enough collateral backing the issued debt. As a result, the stability of the protocol will be compromised. Users can exploit this to take out more debt than they should be able to.

## Proof of Concept

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/main/ebtc-zap-router/src/LeverageZapRouterBase.sol#L232-L255


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The function `LeverageZapRouterBase::_getSwapOperations` is designed to handle swap operations for either opening a new CDP or closing an existing one. Currently, it includes a safeguard called `expectedMinOut` to protect users from receiving less than the minimum expected amount of output tokens (`tokenOut`). However, it does not explicitly check or limit the maximum amount of input tokens (`tokenIn`) that a user can deposit, especially during sudden price increases.

To ensure comprehensive protection against slippage, the function should be updated to include checks for both the maximum acceptable input amount (`tokenIn`) and the minimum acceptable output amount (`tokenOut`). Without these checks, users could end up paying more than necessary if prices suddenly rise, whether due to natural market shifts or artificial manipulation.


## Proof of Concept
Below is the potential scenario how an user got affected with this issue:

A user wants to swap a large amount of stEth for eBTC. Assume the current exchange rate is 1 stETH = 0.0667 eBTC (or 15 stETH = 1 eBTC).
1. User (A) submits their transaction to swap 1500 stETH for 100 eBTC.
2. This transaction is broadcasted to the Ethereum network's mempool, where a malicious node operator (NP) see A's transaction.
3. NP submits his own transaction with a higher gas fee, selling a large amount of stETH for eBTC to drive down the price of stETH. Resulting NP's transaction mined first and decreasing the price of stETH.
4. A's transaction gets processed next, but because the price of stETH is lower, they end up paying more to receive 100 eBTC instead of the originally expected 1500 stETH
5. Meanwhile, NP profits by selling at a high price and buying at a low price, while A experiences a loss in this transaction.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Adding a new paramter `uint256 maxInputAmount;` in `TradeData` struct and enforcing the maximum input amount logic in `_getSwapOperations` and `_getSwapChecks ` functions would help to mitigate this issue.

# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Details 

The _getAdjustCdpParams function it's assumes that the caller has transferred the required collateral before calling the function, and This assumption is critical as the function is proceeds to adjust the CDP without verifying the actual transfer of collateral.
```solidity
  op.tokenToTransferIn = address(stETH);
        // collateral already transferred in by the caller
        op.amountToTransferIn = 0;
        op.operationType = OperationType.AdjustCdpOperation;
        op.OperationData = abi.encode(_cdp);
```
The issue is arise from the assumption that the collateral is already transferred by the caller. This assumption is not verified within the function, is leading to  issues if the collateral is not present. so The function does not include a check in the balance of the collateral token before proceeding with the operation.
## Impact
The function is attempts to proceed with CDP adjustment without sufficient collateral, and this causing the operation to fails so if the operation does not revert, the contract is end up in an incorrect state, leading to inconsistent data and loss of funds

## Proof of Concept
Here is a scenario that show this issue :
- let's Assume that Alice has a CDP with 100 eBTC debt and 50 stETH collateral.
- Alice wants to increase her debt by 50 eBTC, which requires her to add an additional 10 stETH as collateral.
- the contract has the _getAdjustCdpParams function that assumes collateral is transferred by the caller before the function is called.
- The function does not check if the collateral is actually present in the contract.
- Now Alice decides to call the adjustCdpOperation function to increase her debt.
- Alice intends to add 10 stETH as collateral but forgets to transfer the stETH to the contract.
- Alice calls adjustCdpOperation with the following parameters:
```
    cdpId: The ID of Alice's CDP.
    flType: The type of flash loan.
    flAmount: 1000 (amount involved in the flash loan operation).
    cdp: An instance of AdjustCdpOperation with isDebtIncrease set to true, EBTCChange set to 50, stEthBalanceIncrease set to 10, and stEthBalanceDecrease set to 0.
    debt: 100 (current debt).
    coll: 50 (current collateral).
    tradeData: An instance of TradeData with necessary swap operation data.
```
- The adjustCdpOperation function is executed and Inside this function, _getAdjustCdpParams is called to set up the operation parameters and the getAdjustCdpParams assumes the collateral (10 stETH) is already transferred and sets op.amountToTransferIn to 0.
- Since Alice did not transfer the 10 stETH collateral to the contract, the contract does not have sufficient collateral for the operation.
- The function does not verify the presence of the collateral and proceeds with the operation.
- as result The contract attempts to adjust the CDP with insufficient collateral
and it's lead to one of two outcomes:
- The operation fails and reverts due to insufficient collateral during the adjustment process.
- If the operation does not revert, the contract ends up in an incorrect state with an increased debt but without the necessary collateral, potentially leading to an undercollateralized position and financial risk.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-protocol/packages/contracts/contracts/LeverageMacroBase.sol#L393-L430


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Details 
The onFlashLoan function is responsible for handling the callback from a flash loan. While it verifies the initiator and the caller, and  it does not include a check to ensure that the total repayment borrowed amount plus fee is made before the function is completes and this missing in verification is allows the function to return success FLASH_LOAN_SUCCESS even if the loan is underpaid, creating a potential for financial loss.
## Impact
the issue can result the loss of funds to the lender due to incomplete flash loan repayments.
## Proof of Concept
in scenario that Alice  attacker who initiates a flash loan and manipulates the repayment and the Bob is  The protocol or lender providing the flash loan.
- let-s say that the contract is  deployed and configured with necessary dependencies as`borrowerOperations, activePool, ebtcToken,` 
- and Bob provides a flash loan service, implementing the `IERC3156FlashLender` interface.
- now Alice has some tokens to cover the operation fees and Bob has a pool of `eBTC` tokens for flash loans.
- Alice is initiates a flash loan request through contract to borrow `1,000 eBTC` from Bob and the Flash loan fee is set at `1% is 10 eBTC`.
- The flash loan is granted, and `1,000 eBTC` is transferred to the contract and The `onFlashLoan` function is called as the callback.
- Inside the `onFlashLoan` function, the  `_handleOperation` is called with manipulated data and The operation uses some of the borrowed `eBTC` for leveraging actions but ensures not all `eBTC` is used.
- now Alice ensures that only `999 eBTC` is left in the contract balance and The flash loan fee of `10 eBTC` is not included in the balance, making the total repayment short by `11 eBTC` is ` (1,000 borrowed + 10 fee - 999 repaid)`.
- The `onFlashLoan` function is completes without verifying the repayment and 
It returns `FLASH_LOAN_SUCCESS` without checking that the full 
`1,010 eBTC (1,000 borrowed + 10 fee)` is repaid to Bob.

## Tools Used
manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
is still need to add the repayment verification to ensure that the flash loan plus fee is fully repaid before returning FLASH_LOAN_SUCCESS here is an example of fixing :
```solidity
// Missing repayment check
    require(IERC20(token).balanceOf(address(this)) >= amount + fee, "Flash loan repayment is insufficient");
    IERC20(token).transfer(msg.sender, amount + fee);

    return FLASH_LOAN_SUCCESS;
}
```

## Impact
The `adjustCdp` function in the `EbtcLeverageZapRouter` contract allows users to manipulate their CDP's position in the sorted list through the `upperHint` and `lowerHint` parameters without proper validation. This could lead to unfair advantages in liquidation order or other priority-based operations, potentially impacting the fairness and intended functionality of the protocol.

Specifically:
1. Users could potentially position their CDPs more favorably in the queue, affecting liquidation order.
2. This manipulation could result in some users gaining unfair advantages in terms of liquidation risk or redemption priority.
3. The system's intended order of CDPs could be disrupted, leading to unexpected behavior in critical operations.
4. Depending on the implementation of the sorted list, there may be gas cost implications for CDPs at different positions in the queue. Typically, operations on CDPs at the extremes of the list (front or back) might be less expensive in terms of gas compared to those in the middle. This could potentially be exploited by users to optimize their gas costs unfairly.

While this doesn't directly lead to asset loss, it could indirectly impact user positions and system integrity over time.

## Proof of Concept
No code is provided for this PoC due to the complexity of setting up a full test environment. However, the vulnerability can be demonstrated conceptually:

1. The `AdjustCdpParams` struct in `EbtcLeverageZapRouter` includes `upperHint` and `lowerHint` parameters:

```solidity 
struct AdjustCdpParams {
    // ... other parameters ... 
    bytes32 upperHint; 
    bytes32 lowerHint; 
    // ... other parameters ... 
    }
```

2. These parameters are part of the `AdjustCdpParams` struct, which is passed to the `adjustCdp` function without apparent validation, potentially allowing for manipulation of the CDP's position in the sorted list:
```solidity 
function adjustCdp( 
   bytes32 _cdpId, 
   AdjustCdpParams memory _params, 
   bytes calldata _positionManagerPermit, 
   TradeData calldata _tradeData 
   ) external {

      _adjustCdp(
         _cdpId, 
         _params, 
         _positionManagerPermit, 
         _tradeData, 
         _zapStEthBalanceBefore
      );
   }
   ```

3. A malicious user could potentially:
   - Observe the current state of the CDP list
   - Craft specific `upperHint` and `lowerHint` values to position their CDP more favorably
   - Call `adjustCdp` with these crafted hints, potentially moving their CDP to a more advantageous position in the queue

This could be particularly impactful in scenarios where CDP position affects liquidation order or redemption priority.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
1. Implement proper validation for `upperHint` and `lowerHint` parameters in the `EbtcLeverageZapRouter` contract.
2. Consider implementing a mechanism to verify that the provided hints result in a valid and fair position in the CDP queue.
3. Add checks to ensure that the resulting position after applying these hints doesn't violate any system invariants or fairness principles.
4. Consider removing direct user control over these hint parameters and instead calculate them internally based on the CDP's characteristics.
5. If user control over these parameters is necessary, implement strict bounds on how much a CDP's position can change in a single operation.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/main/ebtc-zap-router/src/ZapRouterBase.sol#L34


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Details
In Solidity, the low-level `call` function is used to interact with other contracts or send Ether. It returns two values: a boolean indicating success or failure, and a bytes array containing any returned data. When using `call`, it's crucial to check the boolean return value to ensure the operation succeeded. Failing to do so can lead to silent failures, where a transaction appears to complete successfully even if the underlying operation failed.

In Ethereum, failed calls do not automatically revert the transaction. Instead, they return `false`, allowing the calling contract to handle the failure. If this return value is not checked, the contract may continue execution as if the call succeeded, potentially leading to inconsistent state or unexpected behavior.

## Description:
In the `_depositRawEthIntoLido` function of the ZapRouterBase contract, there is an unchecked low-level `call` used to deposit ETH into the Lido contract:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/main/ebtc-zap-router/src/ZapRouterBase.sol#L34

```solidity
function _depositRawEthIntoLido(uint256 _initialETH) internal returns (uint256) {
    uint256 _balBefore = stEth.balanceOf(address(this));
    payable(address(stEth)).call{value: _initialETH}("");
    uint256 _deposit = stEth.balanceOf(address(this)) - _balBefore;
    return _deposit;
}
```

The `call` function's return value is not checked, which means:

1. If the Lido contract's receive function reverts or if the call fails for any other reason, this function will not revert.
2. The function will continue execution and calculate `_deposit` based on the balance difference, which may be zero or incorrect in case of a failed call.
3. The calling function will receive a potentially incorrect deposit amount and continue execution, assuming the deposit was successful.

## Impact
This issue can lead to:
- Inconsistent contract state
- Loss of user funds if the deposit fails silently
- Incorrect accounting of deposited amounts
- Potential vulnerabilities if other parts of the contract rely on this deposit being successful

## Mitigation

To fix this issue, the return value of the `call` function should be checked, and the transaction should revert if the call fails. Additionally, using a proper interface for the Lido contract would provide better type safety and reduce the risk of errors.

In DeFi protocols interfacing with stETH, it's crucial to accurately account for deposits and distinguish between balance increases due to new deposits and those resulting from rebases. Failure to do so can lead to incorrect accounting, potential exploits, and misrepresentation of user positions.

## Issue
This _depositRawEthIntoLido function may report a successful deposit even if the ETH transfer to Lido fails, due to a coincidental stETH rebase:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/main/ebtc-zap-router/src/ZapRouterBase.sol#L34

```solidity
function _depositRawEthIntoLido(uint256 _initialETH) internal returns (uint256) {
    uint256 _balBefore = stEth.balanceOf(address(this));
    payable(address(stEth)).call{value: _initialETH}("");
    uint256 _deposit = stEth.balanceOf(address(this)) - _balBefore;
    return _deposit;
}
```

The issue arises because:

1. The function checks the stETH balance before and after the attempted deposit to calculate the deposited amount.
2. It doesn't verify if the `call` to Lido's contract succeeded.
3. If a rebase occurs during the execution of this function, the final balance check will show an increase, even if the ETH deposit failed.

## Impact

This can lead to:
- False reporting of successful deposits
- Incorrect accounting of user positions
- Potential loss of user funds if ETH is not actually deposited but recorded as such
- Inconsistencies in the protocol's state and collateral tracking

The impact is severe because:
- Users may believe they've deposited collateral when they haven't
- The protocol may create undercollateralized positions
- It could be exploited by malicious actors to manipulate their position's collateral ratio

To mitigate this issue, the function should:
1. Properly check the return value of the `call` to Lido
2. Use Lido's interface to call the `submit` function directly, which returns the amount of stETH minted
3. Implement a slippage check to ensure the received stETH is within an acceptable range of the expected amount

- Deposit amounts may be recorded higher than the actual user contribution
- Distortion of user position sizes and collateralization ratios
- Potential for strategic exploitation by timing deposits with rebase events
- Overall impairment of the protocol's accounting accuracy and fairness

# Vulnerability details

## Issue
When performing token swaps or conversions, it's crucial to implement slippage protection to guard against unexpected price movements and front-running attacks. This is typically done by specifying a minimum amount of tokens to receive from the conversion. Without such protection, users may receive significantly fewer tokens than expected if the market price shifts unfavorably during the transaction's execution.

## Vulnerability Details
In the ZapRouterBase contract, there are several functions that convert between different forms of ETH-based collateral (ETH, WETH, stETH, wstETH). However, these conversion functions lack checks for minimum received amounts, which could lead to potential losses for users due to slippage or unfavorable price movements.

## Affected functions:
1. _convertWrappedEthToStETH
2. _convertRawEthToStETH
3. _convertWstEthToStETH

These functions perform token conversions without any slippage protection mechanisms. They calculate the received amount after the conversion but do not compare it against any minimum expected value.

For example, in _convertWrappedEthToStETH:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/main/ebtc-zap-router/src/ZapRouterBase.sol#L43

```solidity
uint256 _wETHReiceived = wrappedEth.balanceOf(address(this)) - _wETHBalBefore;
uint256 _rawETHBalBefore = address(this).balance;
IWrappedETH(address(wrappedEth)).withdraw(_wETHReiceived);
uint256 _rawETHConverted = address(this).balance - _rawETHBalBefore;
return _depositRawEthIntoLido(_rawETHConverted);
```

There's no check to ensure that the final amount of stETH received meets a minimum threshold.

## Impact
Without minimum received amount checks, users are exposed to the following risks:

1. Unexpected slippage: If the exchange rate between the token pairs changes unfavorably during the transaction's execution, users may receive significantly fewer tokens than anticipated.

2. Front-running attacks: Malicious actors could exploit this vulnerability by front-running user transactions, manipulating the exchange rate, and causing users to receive fewer tokens.

3. Financial losses: In extreme cases, users could experience substantial financial losses due to receiving far fewer tokens than expected from their conversions.

## Mitigation

Implement slippage protection by adding minimum received amount parameters to these conversion functions and validating the actual received amounts against these minimums.

```sol
    FlashLoanType _flType,
    uint256 _flAmount,
    AdjustCdpOperation memory _cdp,
    uint256 debt,
    uint256 coll,

    uint256 newColl = _cdp._stEthBalanceIncrease > 0 ?

            newDebt, 
            newColl, 
            ICdpManagerData.Status.active,
            _tradeData.collValidationBufferBPS
        ),
        _cdpId
    );

    _sweepEbtc();
}
```

Manual review.

```sol
        _getAdjustCdpParams(_cdp, _tradeData),
        PostOperationCheck.cdpStats,
        _getPostCheckParams(
            _cdpId, 
            newDebt, 
            newColl, 
            ICdpManagerData.Status.active,
            _tradeData.collValidationBufferBPS
        ),
        _cdpId
    );
```

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The `_closeCdpOperation` function is intended to close CDP (Collateralized Debt Position) positions. However, it does not correctly handle the close operation within the `_handleOperation` function.

## Proof of Concept

The `_closeCdpOperation` function calls `_doOperation`, which should in turn call `_handleOperation` with `OperationType.CloseCdpOperation` to manage the closing operation. -           FlashLoanType.eBTC,
```diff
+           FlashLoanType.noFlashloan,
            _debt,
            op,
            PostOperationCheck.isClosed,
            _getPostCheckParams(_cdpId, 0, 0, ICdpManagerData.Status.closedByOwner, 0),
            bytes32(0)
        );
```

## Impact

The `receive` function is designed to block ETH transfers from users except for the wrappedETH address. However, there is a way for users to send ETH with the current implementation.

## Proof of Concept

The contract blocks ETH transfers through the `receive` function but does not block transfers via the `fallback` function. This allows a malicious actor to send ETH to the router using the `fallback` function.

Scenario:
1. A user creates a smart contract and locks some ETH in it.
2. The user then destroys the smart contract using the `selfdestruct` function.
3. The smart contract sends all its ETH to the address specified by the user, which in this case, would be the router.

## Tools Used

- Add a `fallback` function that blocks ETH transactions to prevent ETH from being sent to the router.

```solidity
fallback() external payable {
    require(
            msg.sender == address(wrappedEth),
            "EbtcLeverageZapRouter: only allow Wrapped ETH to send Ether!"
        );
}
```

By implementing this fallback function, the contract will block any ETH transactions that do not come from the specified wrappedETH address, effectively preventing malicious actors from sending ETH to the router using methods like `selfdestruct`.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The `LeverageZapRouterBase` contract currently does not provide the owner with the ability to modify the `zapFeeBPS` and `zapFeeReceiver` parameters. This inflexibility poses a significant risk to the contract's usability and adaptability. If there is a need to update these parameters in response to changing market conditions or organizational changes, the contract will become inoperative, leading to potential financial and operational issues.

## Proof of Concept

In `LeverageZapRouterBase` contract there are no mechanisms for the owner to update the `zapFeeBPS` and `zapFeeReceiver`. This lack of functionality means that the contract cannot adapt to necessary changes, which is a critical flaw in its design.

Scenario Demonstration:
1. Fee Structure Necessity: Suppose the current `zapFeeBPS` is set to 200 basis points. If the market conditions change and a lower fee is required to stay competitive, the contract owner has no means to update this fee, leading to a potential decline in usage.
2. Fee Receiver Update: If the `zapFeeReceiver` address, initially set to `0x123...abc`, becomes compromised or the organization decides to change the recipient address to `0x456...def`, the contract lacks the functionality to make this update. This scenario can result in continued fee distribution to an outdated or compromised address.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

To resolve this critical issue, it is recommended to implement the following functions to provide the owner with the necessary control over these parameters. These functions should be restricted to the contract owner to ensure security:

Proposed Solutions:
1. Function to Update Zap Fee Basis Points:
```solidity
// Function to update the zap fee basis points
function setZapFeeBPS(uint256 newZapFeeBPS) external onlyOwner {
    zapFeeBPS = newZapFeeBPS;
}
```

2. Function to Update Zap Fee Receiver:
```solidity
// Function to update the zap fee receiver address
function setZapFeeReceiver(address newZapFeeReceiver) external onlyOwner {
    require(newZapFeeReceiver != address(0), "Invalid address");
    zapFeeReceiver = newZapFeeReceiver;
}
```

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/main/ebtc-zap-router/src/ZapRouterBase.sol#L19


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

A fixed liquidation reward system can lead to larger debts going unliquidated. For instance, no one would liquidate a 20 ETH debt for a 0.2 ETH reward when they can liquidate a 4 ETH debt for the same reward. Also most liquidators are bots which calculate profit percentages and will avoid liquidating a 20 ETH debt for a 0.2 ETH reward, which yields only a 1% profit.

## Proof of Concept

Scenario 1:
1. Alice opens a position with 4 ETH (valued at $13,219.36 at the current price).
2. Alice's position become liquidatable.
3. Bob notices this and liquidates Alice's position by paying 4 ETH and receives 0.2 ETH as a liquidator reward.

This scenario is typical and frequently occurs.

Scenario 2:
1. Alice opens a position with 20 ETH (valued at $66,078.60 at the current price).
2. Alice's position become liquidatable.
3. Bob notices this but needs 20 ETH ($66,078.60) to liquidate, and he will receive only 0.2 ETH ($660.79).

In Scenario 2, Bob decides not to liquidate Alice's position because the 0.2 ETH reward represents only a 1% profit, which is not attractive enough.

## Tools Used

- Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Implement a dynamic liquidation reward system that adjusts the reward based on the size of the debt. This approach would incentivize liquidators to manage larger debts and prevent significant positions from going underwater.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-zap-router/src/ZapRouterBase.sol#L119-L132


# Vulnerability details

The `_permitPositionManagerApproval()` function attempts to mitigate potential permit front-running using a try-catch block. However, this approach may not fully address the underlying vulnerability and could lead to security risks.

The function calls `borrowerOperations.permitPositionManagerApproval()` with the following parameters:
- `msg.sender` as the owner
- `address(this)` as the position manager
- `IPositionManagers.PositionManagerApproval.OneTime` as the approval type
- Various permit-related parameters (`deadline`, `v`, `r`, `s`)

The try-catch block is implemented as follows: [ZapRouterBase.sol#L119-L132](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-zap-router/src/ZapRouterBase.sol#L119-L132)

```solidity
try
    borrowerOperations.permitPositionManagerApproval(
        msg.sender,
        address(this),
        IPositionManagers.PositionManagerApproval.OneTime,
        _positionManagerPermit.deadline,
        _positionManagerPermit.v,
        _positionManagerPermit.r,
        _positionManagerPermit.s
    )
{} catch {
    /// @notice adding try...catch around to mitigate potential permit front-running
    /// see: https://www.trust-security.xyz/post/permission-denied
}
```

While the intention is to mitigate front-running, this approach may introduce new vulnerabilities/mask important errors.

## Impact
1. The current implementation catches all exceptions without logging or handling them, potentially hiding critical errors or unexpected behavior.
2. Users and developers may assume that the front-running issue is fully resolved, when in reality, it may still be possible under certain conditions.
3. If the permit operation fails silently, it could lead to an inconsistent state between the contract and the user's expectations, potentially causing further issues in subsequent operations.

## Proof of Concept
Consider the following scenario:

1. An attacker monitors the mempool for `_permitPositionManagerApproval()` transactions.
2. When a legitimate transaction is detected, the attacker front-runs it with a higher gas price.
3. The attacker's transaction is processed first, invalidating the legitimate user's permit.
4. When the legitimate transaction is processed, it fails silently due to the try-catch block.
5. The user assumes their permit was successful, but in reality, it wasn't applied.

## Tools Used
Manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
If keeping the try-catch approach, consider logging the error or emitting an event to provide transparency:

```solidity
try
    borrowerOperations.permitPositionManagerApproval(
        msg.sender,
        address(this),
        IPositionManagers.PositionManagerApproval.OneTime,
        _positionManagerPermit.deadline,
        _positionManagerPermit.v,
        _positionManagerPermit.r,
        _positionManagerPermit.s
    )
{} catch Error(string memory reason) {
    emit PermitOperationFailed(msg.sender, reason);
}
```

Or Consider implementing a status check after the permit operation to ensure it was successful, and revert the transaction if not:

```solidity
bool success = borrowerOperations.isPositionManagerApproved(msg.sender, address(this));
require(success, "Position manager approval failed");
```

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-zap-router/src/EbtcLeverageZapRouter.sol#L245-L247


# Vulnerability details

The `EbtcLeverageZapRouter` contract allows users to perform various operations on Collateralized Debt Positions (CDPs) using different forms of Ether as collateral. These operations include opening, adjusting, and closing CDPs. The contract uses a position manager approval mechanism to allow the router to act on behalf of the user. However, the current implementation does not adequately ensure that this approval is revoked after each operation, potentially leaving users vulnerable to unauthorized actions on their CDPs.

In the `_openCdp()` and `_adjustCdp()` functions, the contract attempts to revoke the position manager approval after the operation is completed: [EbtcLeverageZapRouter.sol#L245-L247](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-zap-router/src/EbtcLeverageZapRouter.sol#L245-L247)
```solidity
        if (_positionManagerPermit.length > 0) {
            borrowerOperations.renouncePositionManagerApproval(msg.sender);
        }
```
There is no verification that this revocation was successful. If the revocation fails for any reason, the router would retain approval to act on the user's behalf, which could be exploited in subsequent transactions.

## Impact
If the position manager's approval is not properly revoked, it could lead to several serious consequences:

1. In the worst-case scenario, an attacker could manipulate CDPs to extract value, potentially leading to significant financial losses for users.
2. Users expect their approval to be temporary and specific to a single operation. Lingering approvals violate this expectation and the principle of least privilege.

## Proof of Concept
Consider the following scenario:

1. A user calls `openCdpWithEth()` to open a new CDP.
2. The `_openCdp()` function is executed, which includes granting position manager approval to the router.
3. After the CDP is opened, the contract attempts to revoke the approval, but the revocation fails silently (e.g., due to a gas limit issue or a bug in the `borrowerOperations` contract).
4. The approval remains active, allowing the router to perform future operations on the user's CDP without explicit permission.

## Tools Used
Manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Implement a verification step after revoking the position manager approval. Here's a suggested modification to the `_openCdp()` and `_adjustCdp()` functions
```diff
    if (positionManagerPermit.length > 0) {
        borrowerOperations.renouncePositionManagerApproval(msg.sender);
+  require(!positionManager.isApprovedForAll(address(this), address(ZapRouter)), "Position manager permit not revoked");
        }
    }
```

# Vulnerability details

`LeverageZapRouterBase` contract implements token sweeping mechanisms through the `_sweepEbtc()` and `_sweepStEth()` functions. These functions are designed to transfer any remaining tokens from the contract to the caller after operations. However, the implementation of these sweeping functions is inconsistent across different operations, **_violating the invariant that the `ZapRouter` should not hold any tokens after each operation (aside from rounding)._**

Specifically, in the `_adjustCdpOperation()` function, while `_sweepEbtc()` is called,` _sweepStEth()` is notably absent: [LeverageZapRouterBase.sol#L161-L163](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-zap-router/src/LeverageZapRouterBase.sol#L161-L163)
```solidity
function _adjustCdpOperation( 
    bytes32 _cdpId, 
    FlashLoanType _flType, 
    uint256 _flAmount, 
    AdjustCdpOperation memory _cdp, 
    uint256 debt, 
    uint256 coll, 
    TradeData calldata _tradeData
 ) internal { // ... 
    _sweepEbtc();
// sweepStEth happens outside of this call
```
This inconsistency in token sweeping could lead to stETH tokens being left in the contract after certain operations, violating the stated invariant and potentially causing accounting issues or unexpected behavior in subsequent operations.

## Impact
Violation of the contract's invariant that it should not hold tokens after operations
Accounting discrepancies in subsequent operations
Possible loss of user funds if tokens are left in the contract and not properly accounted for

1. User initiates an `adjustCdp` operation that involves stETH
2. The `_adjustCdpOperation()` function is called
3. The operation completes, and `_sweepEbtc()` is called
4. Any remaining stETH is not swept, as `_sweepStEth()` is not called within this function
5. The contract retains a balance of stETH, violating the invariant

Manual review

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-zap-router/src/EbtcLeverageZapRouter.sol#L459-L466
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-zap-router/src/invariants/ZapRouterPropertiesDescriptions.sol#L17-L18


# Vulnerability details

`EbtcZapRouter` contract, which inherits from `ZapRouterBase`, is designed to facilitate various operations involving CDPs (Collateralized Debt Positions) and different forms of Ethereum (ETH, stETH, wstETH). One of the key invariants of this contract, as stated in [ZapRouterPropertiesDescriptions.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-zap-router/src/invariants/ZapRouterPropertiesDescriptions.sol#L17-L18), is that the `ZapRouter` should not hold any tokens after each operation, except for potential rounding issues.

The contract implements a mechanism to transfer any remaining stETH back to the caller after operations: [EbtcLeverageZapRouter.so#L459-465](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-zap-router/src/EbtcLeverageZapRouter.sol#L459-L466)
```solidity
if (_zapStEthBalanceDiff > 0) {
    _transferStEthToCaller(
        _cdpId,
        EthVariantZapOperationType.AdjustCdp,
        _params.useWstETHForDecrease,
        _zapStEthBalanceDiff
    );
}
```
This mechanism aligns with the invariant described in [ZapRouterPropertiesDescriptions.sol#L17-L18](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-zap-router/src/invariants/ZapRouterPropertiesDescriptions.sol#L17-L18)
```solidity
    string constant ZR_06 =
        "ZR-06: The balance of wstETH in the ZapRouter should never change after creation";
```
However, the contract lacks similar checks and transfer mechanisms for other tokens that might be involved in operations, particularly `eBTC`. This could lead to a scenario where `non-stETH` tokens are inadvertently retained in the contract after operations, violating the intended invariant.

## Impact
* **Violation of contract invariant**: The ZapRouter may retain non-stETH tokens, contradicting the principle that it should not hold any tokens after operations.
* If tokens are retained in the contract, users may lose access to these funds.
* **Increased attack surface:** Accumulated tokens in the contract could become a target for potential exploits.

## Proof of Concept
1. A user operates using the ZapRouter that involves both stETH and eBTC.
2. When the operation is complete, the contract checks for and returns any remaining stETH to the user.
3. a small amount of eBTC remains in the contract due to rounding errors or unforeseen circumstances.
4. The contract has no mechanism to detect or return this eBTC balance.
5. Over time, as multiple users perform operations, eBTC accumulates in the contract.

## Tools Used
Manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
1.  Implement a general token sweeping mechanism that checks for balances of all relevant tokens (stETH, eBTC, etc.) after each operation.
2. Extend the existing `_transferStEthToCaller()` function to handle multiple token types, or create separate functions for each token type.
3. Add a public function that allows the contract owner or users to sweep any remaining tokens to their rightful owners.
```solidity
function sweepTokens(address[] memory tokens) external {
    for (uint i = 0; i < tokens.length; i++) {
        IERC20 token = IERC20(tokens[i]);
        uint256 balance = token.balanceOf(address(this));
        if (balance > 0) {
            token.transfer(msg.sender, balance);
        }
    }
}
```
This function should be called at the end of each operation or made available for users to call if they suspect tokens have been left in the contract.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-zap-router/src/LeverageZapRouterBase.sol#L267-L270


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The collateral validation buffer checking logic is flawed, it provides no slippage protection and brings liquidation risk to user.

## Proof of Concept
When a user calls to open a CDP, [_openCdpOperation()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-zap-router/src/LeverageZapRouterBase.sol#L165-L170) is called and `PostCheckParams` is generated and passed to [_doOperation(https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-protocol/packages/contracts/contracts/LeverageMacroBase.sol#L167-L174)], and is used to check against the actual CDP status.
```
        _doOperation(
            FlashLoanType.stETH,
            _flAmount,
            op,
            PostOperationCheck.openCdp,
@>          _getPostCheckParams(
                _cdpId,
                _cdp.eBTCToMint,
                stETH.getSharesByPooledEth(_cdp.stETHToDeposit),
                ICdpManagerData.Status.active,
                _tradeData.collValidationBufferBPS
            ),
            _cdpId
        );
```
This `PostCheckParams` is crafted as below: 
```
            PostCheckParams({
                expectedDebt: CheckValueAndType({value: _debt, operator: Operator.equal}),
@>              expectedCollateral: CheckValueAndType({
@>                  value:  _totalCollateral * _collValidationBuffer / BPS,
@>                  operator: Operator.gte
@>              }),
                cdpId: _cdpId,
                expectedStatus: _status
            });
```
We can see the value of `expectedCollateral` is `_totalCollateral * _collValidationBuffer / BPS`, and the operator is `Operator.gte`. Later `expectedCollateral` is used to [check against the actual CDP collateral](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-badger/blob/9173558ee1ac8a78a7ae0a39b97b50ff0dd9e0f8/ebtc-protocol/packages/contracts/contracts/LeverageMacroBase.sol#L222).

Assuming `_totalCollateral = 100e18` and `_collValidationBuffer = 10500`, then `expectedCollateral = 105e18`, because `Operator.gte` is assigned for the check, it means the actual collateral can be any value no more than `105e18`, and there is no slippage protection (collateral might be affected by things like rebase etc), results in the actual collateral is lower than expected. Since debt is fixed, less collateral means lower ICR, this brings more liquidation risk to the user.

In addition to that, when opens a CDP, `_stEthDepositAmount` is used to calculate `expectedCollateral`, however, in [BorrowerOperations](https://etherscan.io/address/0xd366e016Ae0677CdCE93472e603b75051E022AD0#code#F1#L456) the actual CDP collateral is calculated based on the net stEth balance, this inconsistency may prevent transaction from reverting when it should be.


## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The current collateral validation buffer logic is a bit convoluted and provides no slippage control.

It is recommended to refactor the logic and use `Operator.lte` instead, e.g. `collValidationBufferBPS = 9000` indicates the actual collateral should not be less than `_stEthDepositAmount * 90%`.

As for the inconsistency:
```diff
    function _openCdp(
        uint256 _debt,
        bytes32 _upperHint,
        bytes32 _lowerHint,
        uint256 _stEthLoanAmount,
        uint256 _stEthMarginAmount,
        uint256 _stEthDepositAmount,
        bytes calldata _positionManagerPermit,
        TradeData calldata _tradeData
    ) internal nonReentrant returns (bytes32 cdpId) {
        ...

        cdp.eBTCToMint = _debt;
        cdp._upperHint = _upperHint;
        cdp._lowerHint = _lowerHint;
-       cdp.stETHToDeposit = _stEthDepositAmount;
+       cdp.stETHToDeposit = _stEthDepositAmount - LIQUIDATOR_REWARD;
        cdp.borrower = msg.sender;

        ...
    }
```














## Assessed type
